passage: Monday. Jatin, nine, finished the fractions sheet in four minutes, then spent the rest of maths drawing black holes in his rough book. When one spiral came out lopsided, he tore the page out and crumpled it. "It has to be perfect," he muttered. Wednesday. At recess he tried to tell two boys about how stars die. They ran off to play catch. Jatin sat on the steps alone, kicking the gravel. The next Saturday. His mother, Vasudha, did not buy the advanced science book he asked for. Instead she took him to the park with a cricket bat and a torn old kite. He got the kite stuck in a tree, laughed until he hiccupped, and fell asleep in the auto home with his head on her arm.

qa.q: How long did Jatin take to finish the fractions sheet?
qa.a: Four minutes.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel at recess when the boys ran off, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt lonely and left out; he sat on the steps alone, kicking the gravel.

qa.q: What choice did Vasudha make on Saturday, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She chose a park trip with a bat and kite instead of another science book, giving him play and comfort, not just more learning.

qa.q: How might the boys at recess see Jatin differently if they played with him?
qa.a: They might find he laughs and plays like any nine-year-old, not only someone who talks about stars.

grounding: It shows a child far ahead in ideas who is bored, perfectionistic and lonely, and a mother who nurtures the whole child through play and comfort.

passage: "Chetan, you want to know about bright children? Sit, I'll tell you about me. At eight I was the girl doing my elder brother's algebra homework for fun. Teachers loved me. But you know what I cried about every night? Losing at hopscotch. And being called 'the professor' at recess, so no one picked me for their team. I was bored in class and lonely outside it. My father noticed. He didn't buy me more books. He sat with me in the evenings and let me win at ludo sometimes, and some days he didn't. He asked about my friends before he asked about marks. He took me to the river to throw stones. So when you teach that clever girl in your class, don't only give her harder sums. Ask who she plays with." Indu smiled and passed him the jaggery.

qa.q: What did Indu cry about every night as a child?
qa.a: Losing at hopscotch, and being called 'the professor' at recess.

qa.q: What does Indu remember feeling as a bright eight-year-old?
qa.a: She remembers feeling bored in class and lonely outside it, even though teachers loved her.

qa.q: What advice does Indu give Chetan about the clever girl in his class?
qa.a: Not to give her only harder sums, but to ask who she plays with and care for her as a whole child.

qa.q: How did Indu's father show he saw more than her marks?
qa.a: He played ludo with her, asked about her friends before marks, and took her to throw stones at the river.

grounding: An elder recalls being a child far ahead in ideas who was also lonely and needed play and comfort, nurtured as a whole child by her father.

subtype: Teacher noticing a restless bright child [Observer]
passage: I'm Jagdish, and I teach Class 5. Let me describe Naveen, because the staffroom keeps asking. He finishes the maths worksheet in ten minutes. Then he asks things like, "Sir, why is zero even?" or "Who decided a week has seven days?" By minute fifteen he's balancing his bottle on his head and the back row is laughing. At first I gave him two more worksheets. He did them in eight minutes and the bottle came out again. So last week I tried something else. I gave him one open question: "Find three ways to prove zero is even, and one way someone might argue it isn't." He worked for the whole period, then asked to present it. The bottle stayed in his bag. His questions now go up on a board by the window.

qa.q: What question did Jagdish give Naveen last week?
qa.a: Find three ways to prove zero is even, and one way someone might argue it isn't.

qa.q: Why might Naveen balance his bottle on his head by minute fifteen?
qa.a: He seems bored once he has finished early, and the fooling around fills the empty time.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Extra worksheets only added more of the same; one deeper, open question kept Naveen interested for the whole period.

qa.q: How might the back row see Naveen once his questions go up on the board?
qa.a: They may see him as someone with interesting questions rather than just the class clown.

grounding: A teacher describes a pupil who finishes early, asks probing questions and then disrupts, and finds that depth and respect for his questions keep interest alive.

subtype: Teacher noticing a restless bright child [Observer]
passage: Tuesday. Dhruv, eleven, finished the plant worksheet first, then asked Avni Ma'am, "But why don't plants fall over when they grow toward the light?" She said, "Not now, Dhruv," and handed him another worksheet. He folded it into a paper plane and flew it across the room. Thursday. Avni had thought about it. When Dhruv finished early, she said, "Your question from Tuesday. Want to test it?" She gave him a bean seedling, a shoebox and a torch. He spent the lesson cutting a window in the box. The following Monday. Dhruv presented his bent seedling to the class, explaining every step. When Suhail asked a question, Dhruv said, "Good question. I don't know yet." Avni noticed no paper planes all week.

qa.q: What did Avni give Dhruv on Thursday?
qa.a: A bean seedling, a shoebox and a torch.

qa.q: What does Dhruv flying the worksheet as a paper plane suggest he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt brushed off and bored when his question was set aside for more of the same work.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Avni's approach?
qa.a: She took his earlier question seriously and gave him a deeper experiment instead of an extra worksheet.

qa.q: How might the class experience lessons differently after the experiment?
qa.a: They get a calmer room without paper planes and hear a classmate's real investigation, and even their own questions are welcomed.

grounding: It shows a teacher who notices a bright pupil finishing early, asking probing questions and disrupting, and who keeps his interest alive with depth, not extra workload.

passage: Week one. In the Class 10 physics test, Sachin knew every answer. He left two blank on purpose. When the boys joked about the "topper nerd" in the next row, he laughed along and felt sick. Week two. His teacher sent him to a weekend science camp in the city. There he met Bidisha, who argued with him for an hour about whether time really exists. Neither of them had to pretend. On the bus home, Sachin realised he hadn't felt that light in months. Week three. He got a plain, middling mark in the art project and waited for the old panic. It didn't come. His mentor at the camp had told him, "You don't need to be top in everything. Be curious." He showed his mother the lopsided pot and they both laughed.

qa.q: Who did Sachin argue with about whether time really exists?
qa.a: Bidisha, at the weekend science camp.

qa.q: Why did Sachin feel sick while laughing along with the boys?
qa.a: He was hiding his ability to belong, and pretending went against who he is.

qa.q: What turning point eased the pressure on Sachin?
qa.a: Meeting like-minded Bidisha at the camp, and a mentor telling him he doesn't need to be top in everything.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have experienced the argument with Sachin?
qa.a: Bidisha probably enjoyed it too, finding someone who could match that curiosity without either of them pretending.

grounding: It shows a gifted teen who hides his ability to belong and feels pressure to be top, relieved by like-minded peers, a mentor and permission to be average sometimes.

passage: "You think you're the first one to feel this, Preeti?" Aparna Masi put down her knitting. "When I was your age, I was the girl who always topped. Every exam, every year. Teachers read my essays aloud. And do you know what I did at lunch? Ate alone in the library. I told myself it was because I liked books. Partly true. Mostly, I didn't know how to talk to the others. Then one exam I came fourth, and I cried so hard I threw up. Fourth! My science teacher found me. She said, 'Aparna, you are allowed to be ordinary on a Tuesday.' I laughed for the first time that week. She took me to the chess club, where no one cared about my rank. So if you get a B on this test, beta, the world keeps turning."

qa.q: Where did Aparna eat lunch as a teenager?
qa.a: Alone in the library.

qa.q: What does crying so hard after coming fourth show about how Aparna felt then?
qa.a: It shows she felt that every result had to be top, and anything less felt like failure.

qa.q: Which moment helped teenage Aparna the most?
qa.a: Her teacher told her she was allowed to be ordinary and took her to the chess club, where no one cared about her rank.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel hearing this story from her Masi?
qa.a: Preeti may feel less alone and less pressured, knowing someone Preeti admires felt the same and came through it.

grounding: An elder recalls being a gifted teen who felt out of step and pressured to top everything, relieved by a mentor, a like-minded club and permission to be ordinary.

passage: I've lived next door to Leela since we were six, so I know her family well. I'm Zainab. Her father is proud of her, really proud. Every test mark goes onto the family group within minutes. At dinner the talk is ranks, olympiads, which coaching batch next. When she got 94 in maths, he asked, "Who got the extra marks?" Last month on the terrace, Leela said, very quietly, "If I stop being clever, I think they'd stop liking me." I didn't know what to say. I just sat next to her. Then something changed. Her aunt must have said something. On Sunday I heard her father through the wall asking Leela to teach him the song she'd been humming. No marks, just singing badly together. Leela was laughing, properly laughing.

qa.q: Where does Leela's father post every test mark?
qa.a: Onto the family group within minutes.

qa.q: What was Leela afraid of, based on what she said on the terrace?
qa.a: She was afraid her family would stop liking her if she stopped being clever.

qa.q: What small change seemed to help Leela at home?
qa.a: Her father spent time singing with her with no talk of marks, showing interest in her beyond her ability.

qa.q: How does Zainab seem to feel watching Leela's situation?
qa.a: Zainab seems worried and unsure what to say, but stays close, and is glad to hear Leela laughing on Sunday.

grounding: A neighbour sees a gifted girl whose proud father pushes constant achievement until she feels loved only for being clever, and how valuing her beyond ability helps.

passage: Saturday. At his cousin's wedding, Yogesh put an arm around Gopika and told every uncle, "Our genius. Ninety-eight in science!" Gopika smiled until her cheeks hurt. Wednesday. The results came. Second rank. She went straight to the bathroom and cried with the tap running. When she came out she asked, "Papa, would you still love me if I was just ordinary?" Yogesh stared at her. He didn't answer. He hadn't known she thought that. The next Sunday. He took her for cutting chai at the corner stall. "I watched you with your little cousin at the wedding," he said. "You carried her when she was scared of the band. That's what I'm proudest of." He never mentioned the rank. Gopika leaned her head on his shoulder.

qa.q: What did Yogesh tell every uncle at the wedding?
qa.a: Our genius. Ninety-eight in science!

qa.q: What does Gopika's question to her father show she was worried about?
qa.a: It shows she worried his love depended on her marks and brilliance.

qa.q: What turning point did Yogesh choose after hearing her question?
qa.a: He took her for chai and praised her kindness to her cousin, not mentioning the rank at all.

qa.q: What was the wedding like for Gopika while Yogesh boasted?
qa.a: She smiled until her cheeks hurt, feeling shown off for her marks rather than just being herself.

grounding: It shows a proud father pushing achievement, a daughter who feels loved only for brilliance, and how valuing her beyond ability comforts her.

passage: Monday. Samir won the college data-modelling contest by a mile. The same evening, his sister Farida found the scholarship form, unsigned, under a pile of chip packets. The deadline had passed at noon. Thursday. Farida came home in tears after a bad viva. Samir listed five ways to prepare better next time. She snapped, "I didn't ask you to fix me!" and slammed her door. He sat in the corridor, puzzled and hot-faced. The next Sunday. Samir wrote two lists on the whiteboard: things I'm great at, and things I'm still learning. Organising and "knowing when someone just wants listening" went on the second. He didn't erase them. He set phone reminders for every form. Then he knocked on Farida's door. "Do you want advice, or just company?" "Company," she said, and moved over.

qa.q: What did Samir win on Monday?
qa.a: The college data-modelling contest, by a mile.

qa.q: How did Samir feel after Farida slammed her door, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt confused and embarrassed; he sat in the corridor puzzled and hot-faced.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Samir?
qa.a: He listed his strengths and gaps without erasing them, set reminders for forms, and asked Farida whether she wanted advice or company.

qa.q: How might Farida see Samir's question 'advice, or just company?'
qa.a: She likely feels understood, since he is now asking what she needs instead of trying to fix her.

grounding: It shows a young adult brilliant at analysis who struggles with organisation and emotional skills, and who looks at strengths and gaps without shame to work on each.

passage: "Jeevan, sit down. You missed one deadline, you didn't set the lab on fire. When I was your age, I could build a model from any messy data in a night. Our professor called me the sharpest in the batch. And I missed three project meetings in one month because I never wrote anything down. Once I made a junior cry by telling her, flat, that her code was useless. I didn't even notice until someone told me. I felt ashamed, and I wanted to hide in the numbers. My supervisor didn't let me. She said, 'Nilesh, you have a brilliant head and a messy diary. Both are true. Fix the diary.' So I got a paper planner, and I started asking juniors, 'Can I give feedback now?' Thirty years later, I still use the planner."

qa.q: What did Nilesh's supervisor say to fix?
qa.a: The diary.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel on learning about making a junior cry?
qa.a: Nilesh felt ashamed and wanted to hide in the numbers.

qa.q: What steps did Nilesh take that Jeevan could copy?
qa.a: Nilesh got a paper planner and began asking before giving feedback, working on each gap without shame.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel hearing this from a senior colleague?
qa.a: Jeevan may feel less ashamed about the missed deadline, seeing that a respected expert had the same gaps and fixed them.

grounding: A senior colleague recalls being brilliant at analysis but weak at organisation and emotional skills, and learning to see strengths and gaps without shame.

passage: In a park in Krakow, Marek, five, spotted a dog as big as a pony. "M-m-mama! A d-d-d-dog! It's a b-b-b-big one and it has a sss-sss-spotty tongue!" His face scrunched on the hard sounds, but he kept going, bouncing on his toes. Dalia crouched beside him. She did not say "slow down." She did not finish his words. She just waited, eyes on his, smiling. "Can I p-p-pat it?" "Let's ask the owner," Dalia said calmly. The dog licked Marek's hand, and he shrieked with delight.

qa.q: What did Marek say the dog's tongue looked like?
qa.a: Spotty.

qa.q: How can you tell Marek was excited rather than upset?
qa.a: He kept going, bouncing on his toes, and shrieked with delight when the dog licked him.

qa.q: Which of Dalia's choices helped Marek most?
qa.a: She waited calmly with her eyes on his, without saying slow down or finishing his words.

qa.q: What would change if Dalia had finished Marek's sentences for him?
qa.a: Marek might learn that his words were not worth waiting for, and the happy moment might turn into tension.

grounding: It shows a young child who repeats and stretches sounds when excited, with some facial tension, and a mother whose calm listening helps.

passage: At the kindergarten's Monday news circle, Sahil waved his hand so hard he nearly fell over. "I have a b-b-b-baby s-s-sister! She's sss-so small! She has t-t-t-tiny f-f-fingers!" His forehead tightened on each hard word, but Sahil didn't seem to notice. He was too busy showing how tiny with his thumb and finger. Pema Miss nodded and waited, never hurrying him. "What's her name?" "M-m-m-Mishti!" "Mishti. What a sweet name. What does she do all day?" "She s-s-sleeps and cries and sleeps." The circle giggled, and so did Sahil.

qa.q: What is the name of Sahil's baby sister?
qa.a: Mishti.

qa.q: How can you tell Sahil wasn't worried about his speech?
qa.a: He didn't seem to notice the stretched sounds and was too busy showing how tiny his sister is.

qa.q: What did Pema Miss do that helped Sahil share his news?
qa.a: She nodded, waited without hurrying him and asked questions to keep him talking.

qa.q: How do the other children in the circle experience Sahil's news?
qa.a: They enjoy his story like any other and giggle with him about the baby sleeping and crying.

grounding: It shows a young child who repeats sounds with some tension when excited, is unaware of it, and a teacher whose calm listening helps.

passage: After football in a London park, Kwame and Diego sat on the bench with orange slices. "D-d-d-do you know what my g-g-g-grandad did?" Diego started. A bigger boy walking past said, "Just take a breath, mate." Kwame didn't look away from Diego. He kept chewing and waited, like it was the most normal thing in the world. "H-he fell in the p-p-pond. With his sh-sh-shoes on!" Kwame laughed so hard orange juice ran down his chin. "Was he okay?" "He was s-s-soggy!" Diego grinned. Kwame threw his peel in the bin. "Tell me the rest tomorrow."

qa.q: Where did Diego's grandad fall?
qa.a: In the pond, with his shoes on.

qa.q: What does Diego's grin at the end suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt happy and respected, because Kwame listened to the whole story and enjoyed it.

qa.q: What did Kwame do that a wise listener would do?
qa.a: He kept his eyes on Diego, waited without finishing his words, and responded to the story itself.

qa.q: How might Diego have felt about the bigger boy's comment?
qa.a: He may have felt hurried or singled out, since being told to take a breath treats his talking as a problem.

grounding: A peer meets a friend's stuttering by waiting, not completing sentences and not telling him to take a breath, treating him as a full conversation partner.

passage: At the community centre library, five-year-old Jomon came up to the desk holding his father's hand. "C-c-c-can I have the b-b-b-book with the..." His lips pressed together and nothing came for a moment. Simran, the librarian, stayed kneeling at his height. She didn't guess. She didn't say "take your time." She just kept looking at him kindly and waited. "...the r-r-red tractor." "The red tractor book! We have two. One with flaps, one without. Which do you want?" "F-flaps!" "Flaps it is." She stamped his card and handed it to him, not to his father. Jomon hugged the book to his chest.

qa.q: Which book did Jomon want?
qa.a: The red tractor book, the one with flaps.

qa.q: What does Jomon hugging the book suggest he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt proud and happy that he asked for it himself and got what he wanted.

qa.q: Which of Simran's choices showed respect for Jomon's pace?
qa.a: She waited without guessing or saying take your time, then gave him a real choice and handed the book to him directly.

qa.q: What would change for Jomon if Simran had guessed the book for him?
qa.a: He might feel his words didn't matter, and his father might end up speaking for him.

grounding: An adult meets a child's stuttering by waiting without completing sentences or giving advice, treating him as a full conversation partner.

passage: Jahnavi knew every answer in Class 5, but she dreaded roll call. Her name began with a sound that got stuck. So each morning, when Vandana Ma'am called "Jahnavi?", she said "Present" through a cough, or just raised her hand. In reading hour she swapped words to dodge the hard ones: "big" instead of "huge", "later" instead of "tomorrow". Sometimes the sentence came out strange. A boy at the back started copying her, "J-j-j-jahnavi," and she stared at her desk until her eyes burned. That night her mother held her and listened to all of it. On Saturday they went to a qualified speech therapist near the station, who showed Jahnavi how to ease into a word gently. On Monday, her mother spoke to Vandana Ma'am about the boy.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi say instead of 'huge' in reading hour?
qa.a: Big.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi dread roll call?
qa.a: She feared getting stuck on her own name in front of the class and being laughed at.

qa.q: Which choices by her mother helped?
qa.a: She listened to all of it, took Jahnavi to a qualified speech therapist, and told the teacher about the teasing.

qa.q: How might Vandana Ma'am's classroom change once she knows about the teasing?
qa.a: She can stop the copying and give Jahnavi time, so roll call feels less frightening.

grounding: It shows a child who avoids reading aloud, swaps words to dodge hard sounds and dreads being called on, worsened by teasing and helped by speech therapy.

passage: "Omkar, stay a minute?" Gurleen Ma'am said as the others filed out. "D-d-did I do something?" "No. I noticed you didn't volunteer for the play reading. Would you like to tell me why?" He twisted his tie. "I g-get stuck. And then R-Rohit's gang does the noise." "Thank you for telling me. That noise stops today; I'll speak to them. Now, what would make reading easier for you?" "If I kn-know which part the day before. And if nobody hurries me." "Done. I'll give you your part tomorrow, and I'll wait as long as it takes. Your speech therapist on Wednesdays, would it help if I knew what she's practising with you?" Omkar looked up for the first time. "Yeah. That would help." "Good. I'd like to hear your part in the play."

qa.q: On which day does Omkar see his speech therapist?
qa.a: On Wednesdays.

qa.q: Why did Omkar avoid volunteering for the play reading?
qa.a: He was afraid of getting stuck and of Rohit's gang making the noise to mock him.

qa.q: What steps did Gurleen Ma'am agree to take?
qa.a: Stop the teasing, give him his part the day before, wait as long as it takes, and learn what the therapist is practising.

qa.q: How does Omkar's attitude change during the talk?
qa.a: At first he twists his tie and avoids her eyes, but by the end he looks up and agrees it would help.

grounding: It shows a child who dreads reading aloud because of stuttering and teasing, and a teacher who allows time and works alongside his speech therapist.

passage: Sunaina had written the call on a sticky note: "Hello, I'd like to order a chocolate cake for Saturday, with 'Happy Birthday Mummy' on top." She had said it in her head maybe forty times. Her thoughts were perfectly clear. It was the moment after the first word that scared her: the pause, the shopkeeper's sigh, the "Hello? Hello?" and the click. "Just message them," Zeenat said, flopping on the bed. "They only take calls." Sunaina stared at the phone. Her hands were cold. She dialled. "H-h-hello. I'd like to order a ch... a chocolate cake." The woman at the bakery didn't sigh. She said, "Sure, what name on top?" Afterwards Sunaina lay back, hands shaking, and grinned at the ceiling. Zeenat threw a pillow at her. "Told you."

qa.q: What did Sunaina want written on top of the cake?
qa.a: Happy Birthday Mummy.

qa.q: What was Sunaina afraid of before making the call?
qa.a: She was afraid of the pause after the first word and the shopkeeper sighing or hanging up, not of what she wanted to say.

qa.q: What made the call a turning point for Sunaina?
qa.a: She chose to dial despite her fear, and the woman at the bakery waited patiently instead of sighing.

qa.q: How might the bakery woman's patience affect Sunaina's next call?
qa.a: It might make the next call feel less frightening, since she now knows some listeners simply wait.

grounding: It shows a teenager who rehearses and avoids phone calls although her thoughts are clear, whose stress is mostly about how others will react.

passage: "Ujjwal? It's midnight. Who are you talking to?" "Nobody, Chetan-bhaiya. Go to sleep." "You're talking to the mirror." Ujjwal sighs. "I'm practising the debate intro. Seventeen times now." "You know the topic better than anyone. I heard you at dinner." "At dinner it's you and Mummy. In class it's forty people, and when I get stuck on the first word, they look at each other. That look. So I just don't put my hand up." "You've got answers in your head all day and you don't say them?" "Every day." Chetan sits on the edge of the bed. "That sounds exhausting." "It is. The words aren't the hard part. The faces are." "Then practise on me tomorrow. I'll do the most boring face in the world." Ujjwal laughs despite himself. "Deal."

qa.q: How many times had Ujjwal practised the debate intro?
qa.a: Seventeen times.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal mean when he says 'The faces are' the hard part?
qa.a: He means he fears how classmates react when he gets stuck, more than the speaking itself.

qa.q: What small step does Chetan offer that could help?
qa.a: He offers to let Ujjwal practise on him tomorrow, with a calm, boring face.

qa.q: What is it like for Chetan to learn his brother stays silent every day?
qa.a: It surprises and saddens him, since he knows Ujjwal is clever, and he realises how tiring it must be.

grounding: It shows a teenager who stays silent in class and rehearses constantly although his thoughts are ready, and whose stress is mostly about others' reactions.

passage: "First thing I say in every presentation now is: 'I'm Wasim, I stutter, and I'll get there.' Then I carry on. Took me three years to say that line. In first year I'd apologise every time I blocked. 'S-sorry, sorry.' I'd end up apologising more than presenting. People would jump in and finish my sentences. Kind, I guess, but it made me feel like a kid. What changed was a support group my speech therapist told me about. Fifteen people on video calls every Thursday. One of them was a lawyer! For the first time I wasn't the only one. Now I slow down on purpose. I pause. I don't say sorry. And I notice who waits. Deepak, my project partner, keeps looking right at me and just waits. Those people make it so much easier."

qa.q: What is the first thing Wasim says in every presentation now?
qa.a: I'm Wasim, I stutter, and I'll get there.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel when people finished Wasim's sentences?
qa.a: Wasim felt treated like a kid, even though the others meant to be kind.

qa.q: What was the turning point that helped Wasim speak with confidence?
qa.a: Joining a support group through the speech therapist, where Wasim was no longer the only one.

qa.q: How does Deepak's way of listening affect Wasim?
qa.a: Deepak keeps looking at Wasim and waits, which makes speaking much easier.

grounding: It shows a young adult who speaks openly about stuttering, slows down without apologising, and is helped by patient listeners and a support group.

passage: I'm Manoj. I sat beside Jahnavi on her first client call last month, and I still think about it. She'd joined our team two weeks before. When the call started, she said, clear as anything, "Hi, I'm Jahnavi. I stutter, so sometimes I'll take a moment. The numbers are worth the wait." The client laughed and said, "No problem." Then she walked them through the whole budget. She blocked a couple of times on words starting with "p". She paused, didn't apologise, and carried on. The client kept waiting and nodding. After the call I asked, "Weren't you nervous?" She shrugged. "Less than I used to be. I go to a support group on Thursdays. Makes me feel less alone." The client emailed next day, asking specifically for her.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi say at the start of the call?
qa.a: Hi, I'm Jahnavi. I stutter, so sometimes I'll take a moment. The numbers are worth the wait.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi's shrug and answer suggest about how she feels about speaking now?
qa.a: It suggests she still feels some nerves but is much more confident, helped by the support group.

qa.q: Which of Jahnavi's choices made the call go smoothly?
qa.a: She told the client about her stutter at the start, paused without apologising, and kept going.

qa.q: How did the client respond to Jahnavi's openness?
qa.a: The client laughed kindly, kept waiting and nodding, and later asked for her specifically.

grounding: A colleague describes a young adult who speaks openly about stuttering, pauses without apologising, and is helped by patient listeners and a support group.
